rules.coverage_note: Which PHP files are plugin (or must-use plugin) code. WordPress decides that by location, not by syntax, so the artifact path is the whole of the evidence and no Pack field is involved.
Which PHP files are theme code, by the same path convention. The surface attribute is what tells a reader whether a registration belongs to a plugin or to the active theme.

Which file renders which view. The template hierarchy is WordPress knowledge a PHP Pack cannot have: single.php serves a single post, 404.php the not-found view. The file name is the route, so path.stem answers it, and the View is the shared node that two themes' single.php both reach.

Which files wire behaviour onto WordPress hooks. This is the central WordPress question -- what runs when -- and add_action/add_filter is the only thing that answers it. The hook name and the callback are call arguments, and omega-php publishes no argument field, so the edge is file-to-API rather than file-to-hook.
Which files define extension points of their own. do_action and apply_filters are how a plugin invites other code in, so these are the files a third-party integrator has to read.
Which files define the site's content model -- the custom post types, taxonomies and registered meta that a WordPress site's schema consists of.
Which files register editor blocks, patterns and block styles: the server side of the block editor.
Which files add REST endpoints or fields. The namespace and route are string arguments the Pack does not publish, so this names the file that serves API surface rather than the path it serves.
Which files build the wp-admin surface: menu pages, meta boxes and the Settings API. This is where a site's configuration screens come from.
Which files register shortcodes, widgets, sidebars, nav menus and theme supports -- the things an editor can place on a page.
Which files put scripts and styles on the page. Asset handles are string arguments the Pack does not publish, so the answer is the enqueuing file, which is the file to edit.

Which files read or write persistent site settings -- the options table, transients and theme mods. Keeping this separate from ordinary data access is what makes 'where is this setting touched' answerable.
Which files read or write posts, terms, users and their meta through the WordPress data API rather than SQL.
Which files construct a WordPress query or response object. WP_Query is the idiomatic read path and arrives as call.constructor, a different fact kind from the wp_* functions above.

Which files check a capability or a nonce before acting. A registration with none of these anywhere near it is the shape of a WordPress privilege bug, so the two sets being separately reachable is the point.

Which named PHP function performs a WordPress registration. Most plugins wrap their registrations in a bootstrap function that is itself hooked onto init or plugins_loaded, and the span join to scope.function_body names it without any Pack field. A registration at file top level lies in no function scope and is answered by the file-level rules instead.

Which blocks the project defines. A block.json is one block, and apiVersion is its top-level marker key, so the metadata file's path identifies the block and its directory is the block's source folder. The block's own name and script handles are config values, which omega-json publishes as an attribute the overlay cannot read.

gaps: omega-php publishes no field on any of its templates, so no call argument is visible to the overlay: hook names, callbacks, shortcode tags, option keys, REST namespaces and asset handles are all string arguments and none of them can be materialized.
what is materialized is the file, the enclosing PHP function, the WordPress API each one uses, the theme template hierarchy by file name, and the blocks a block.json declares.

config values in block.json and theme.json are published by omega-json as an attribute, and OverlayFact::field never reads attributes, so a block's own name and script handles stay unreachable until that value moves to fields.
runtime plugin and theme activation order, dynamically composed hook names, callable arrays and closures remain runtime semantics.
